title: What is a Transformer? Self-Attention, Multi-Head Attention and Positional Encoding
description: How the attention-based Transformer processes sequences in parallel, captures long-range dependencies and recovers word order with positional encoding.
content:
**Transformer** is one of the fundamental architectures used in NLP, based on the attention mechanism.

Key advantages:
• Parallelization - self-attention allows the model to process words in parallel, which makes training significantly faster compared to sequential models like RNN.
• Long-range dependencies - self-attention enables the Transformer to effectively capture long-distance dependencies, allowing it to work with large context windows.

Key structures:
• Self-attention mechanism - deals with input contexts and matrices of queries, keys and values and their weighted sum.
• Encoder-decoder network - a simplistic encoder-decoder neural network structure.
• Multi-head attention - allows parallelizing self-attention and applying it to different parts of the input.
• Positional encoding - deals with sequence order information.
• Feedforward neural network - included in both the encoder and the decoder.
• Normalization layers and residual connections - allow scalability and flexibility of the model.

**Self-attention** is a tool that allows the Transformer to capture long-range dependencies in sequences:
• Each word in the input sequence attends to all other words in the same sequence.
• The model learns to assign weights to each word based on its relevance to the others.
• This captures both long-term and short-term dependencies, which is crucial in NLP problems.

**Multi-head attention** allows the Transformer to recognize different patterns and correlations in the input sequence:
• It is used in both the encoder and the decoder.
• Each attention head learns to pay attention to different parts of the input.
• This lets the model capture a spectrum of characteristics and dependencies.

**Positional encoding**:
• The Transformer processes input sequences in parallel, so it lacks information about word order - unlike RNNs or LSTMs - and needs a way to show this information explicitly.
• Positional encoding is applied to the input sequences to provide positional information: relative or absolute positions of each token.
• Encodings are typically learned and can take several forms, including sine and cosine functions or learned embeddings.
• This allows the model, for example, to distinguish the same word in different positions.
